# The Lorentzian family $\delta_n(x)=\dfrac{n}{\pi}\dfrac{1}{1+n^2x^2}$ is a delta sequence

## Statement

For $n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ define $\delta_n:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$\delta_n(x):=\frac{n}{\pi}\,\frac{1}{1+n^2x^2}.$$
Then $(\delta_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}}$ is a *delta sequence*: it converges to the Dirac delta distribution $\delta$ in the sense of distributions, i.e. for every test function $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,\phi(x)\,dx=\delta(\phi)=\phi(0).$$

Here $\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$ denotes the space of infinitely differentiable functions $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ with compact support, and $\delta\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ is the Dirac delta distribution, $\delta(\phi):=\phi(0)$.

The claim is **true**, and is proved below.

**What is actually used about $\phi$.** Only two properties enter the argument:

* $\phi$ is **bounded**: $M:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|\phi(x)|<\infty$. Indeed, let $K:=\operatorname{supp}\phi$, a compact set. The function $|\phi|$ is continuous, hence attains a finite maximum on $K$ by the extreme value theorem, and $\phi$ vanishes off $K$; so $M=\max_{K}|\phi|<\infty$ (with $M=0$ if $K=\varnothing$).
* $\phi$ is **continuous at $0$** (it is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb{R}$).

---

## Step 0: Conventions on improper integrals; the integrals in question converge

**Convention.** For a function $f$ continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ we write $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{A\to\infty,\;B\to\infty}\int_{-A}^{B}f(x)\,dx$, the two limits being taken independently. We shall use repeatedly the following standard facts.

> **(F1)** If $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|f|<\infty$ (absolute convergence), then $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f$ converges, and for **any** sequences $a_k\to-\infty$, $b_k\to+\infty$ one has $\int_{a_k}^{b_k}f\to\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f$.
>
> *Reason.* $F(x):=\int_0^x f$ satisfies $|F(b)-F(b')|\le\int_{\min(b,b')}^{\max(b,b')}|f|\to0$ as $b,b'\to+\infty$ by the Cauchy criterion for the convergent increasing integral $\int_0^{b}|f|$; hence $\lim_{b\to\infty}F(b)$ exists, and similarly $\lim_{a\to-\infty}F(a)$. The value $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f$ is the difference of these two limits, and any exhaustion $[a_k,b_k]$ with $a_k\to-\infty,\ b_k\to+\infty$ produces it.
>
> **(F2)** If $f\ge0$ is continuous, then $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f$ converges if and only if $\sup_{A>0}\int_{-A}^{A}f<\infty$, in which case the two agree; this is monotonicity of the integral in the interval. In particular the symmetric limit computes the integral.
>
> **(F3)** For an absolutely convergent $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f$ with $f$ continuous, the improper Riemann integral equals the Lebesgue integral of $f$ over $\mathbb{R}$; so the statement to be proved is the same under either reading, and linearity and the splitting $\int_{\mathbb{R}}=\int_{|t|<c}+\int_{|t|\ge c}$ are available.

Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$. Since $1+n^2x^2\ge1>0$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$, $\delta_n$ is defined, continuous and strictly positive on $\mathbb{R}$; in particular it is locally integrable, so it determines a regular distribution $T_{\delta_n}(\phi)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\delta_n\phi$ as soon as this integral converges.

Differentiating, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\pi}\arctan(nx)\right)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{n}{1+n^{2}x^{2}}=\delta_n(x)$, so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, for every $A>0$,
$$\int_{-A}^{A}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\frac{1}{\pi}\bigl[\arctan(nx)\bigr]_{-A}^{A}=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan(nA)\le 1 . \tag{0.1}$$
Since $\delta_n\ge0$, fact (F2) and $\arctan(nA)\to\pi/2$ give convergence together with the value:
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\lim_{A\to\infty}\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan(nA)=1. \tag{0.2}$$
Consequently $|\delta_n(x)\phi(x)|\le M\,\delta_n(x)$ yields $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\delta_n\phi|\le M<\infty$: the integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n\phi$ converges absolutely, so by (F1) and (F3) it is a well-defined number, insensitive to the exhaustion used and the same in the Riemann and Lebesgue senses. Thus $T_{\delta_n}\in\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ is well defined.

## Step 1: Normalisation — each graph encloses unit area

Equation $(0.2)$ says precisely that for every $n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx=\frac{n}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{1+n^{2}x^{2}}=1, \tag{1.1}$$
which is the assertion "the area under each graph is equal to $1$". Taking $n=1$:
$$\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}=1. \tag{1.2}$$

## Step 2: Rescaling

Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ and $A>0$. The map $t\mapsto x=t/n$ is a $C^{1}$ bijection of $[-nA,nA]$ onto $[-A,A]$ with derivative $1/n>0$, and $\phi$ is continuous, so the change-of-variables formula for Riemann integrals over compact intervals gives
$$\int_{-A}^{A}\frac{n}{\pi}\frac{\phi(x)}{1+n^{2}x^{2}}\,dx
=\int_{-nA}^{nA}\frac{n}{\pi}\frac{\phi(t/n)}{1+t^{2}}\cdot\frac{dt}{n}
=\int_{-nA}^{nA}\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\phi(t/n)}{1+t^{2}}\,dt . \tag{2.1}$$
(Here $n^2x^2=t^2$ when $x=t/n$.)

Both improper integrals involved converge absolutely: the left-hand integrand by Step 0; the right-hand integrand because $\bigl|\phi(t/n)/(1+t^{2})\bigr|\le M/(1+t^{2})$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt/(1+t^{2})=\pi<\infty$ by $(1.2)$. Hence, by (F1), letting $A\to\infty$ in $(2.1)$ — the left side along the exhaustion $[-A,A]$, the right side along the exhaustion $[-nA,nA]$, both admissible since $nA\to\infty$ — we obtain
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\phi(t/n)}{1+t^{2}}\,dt . \tag{2.2}$$

## Step 3: The error integral

Multiply $(1.2)$ by the constant $\phi(0)$ and subtract it from $(2.2)$. Since $t\mapsto\phi(t/n)/(1+t^{2})$ and $t\mapsto\phi(0)/(1+t^{2})$ are both absolutely integrable, linearity of the integral applies and gives, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx-\phi(0)
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)}{1+t^{2}}\,dt=:E_n . \tag{3.1}$$
It remains to prove $E_n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.

## Step 4: $E_n\to0$

If $M=0$ then $\phi\equiv0$, so $E_n=0$ for all $n$ and there is nothing to prove. Assume $M>0$ and let $\varepsilon>0$ be given.

*Choice of $\eta$.* By continuity of $\phi$ at $0$ there is $\eta>0$ with
$$|x|<\eta\ \Longrightarrow\ |\phi(x)-\phi(0)|<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. \tag{4.1}$$

*Choice of $N$.* Since $\arctan s\to\pi/2$ as $s\to+\infty$ and $\eta>0$ is fixed, $\frac{4M}{\pi}\bigl(\frac\pi2-\arctan(n\eta)\bigr)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$; choose $N\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ with
$$n\ge N\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{4M}{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan(n\eta)\right)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. \tag{4.2}$$

*Estimate.* Fix $n\ge N$. Splitting the absolutely convergent integral in $(3.1)$ at $|t|=n\eta$ (legitimate by (F3)) and using the triangle inequality,
$$\pi\,|E_n|\le \underbrace{\int_{\{|t|<n\eta\}}\frac{|\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)|}{1+t^{2}}\,dt}_{=:I_1}\;+\;\underbrace{\int_{\{|t|\ge n\eta\}}\frac{|\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)|}{1+t^{2}}\,dt}_{=:I_2}.$$

**Bound for $I_1$.** If $|t|<n\eta$ then $|t/n|<\eta$, so $(4.1)$ gives $|\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)|<\varepsilon/2$. Hence
$$I_1\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{\{|t|<n\eta\}}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\cdot\pi .$$

**Bound for $I_2$.** For every $t$, $|\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)|\le|\phi(t/n)|+|\phi(0)|\le2M$. Moreover, by symmetry of the integrand and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
$$\int_{\{|t|\ge n\eta\}}\frac{dt}{1+t^{2}}=2\lim_{B\to\infty}\bigl[\arctan t\bigr]_{n\eta}^{B}=2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan(n\eta)\right).$$
Therefore, by $(4.2)$,
$$I_2\le 2M\cdot2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan(n\eta)\right)=4M\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan(n\eta)\right)<\pi\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.$$

Adding the two bounds, $\pi|E_n|<\pi\varepsilon/2+\pi\varepsilon/2=\pi\varepsilon$, i.e.
$$|E_n|<\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }n\ge N .$$
Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $\lim_{n\to\infty}E_n=0$.

## Conclusion

By $(3.1)$ and Step 4, for every $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{n}{\pi}\,\frac{\phi(x)}{1+n^{2}x^{2}}\,dx=\phi(0)=\delta(\phi),$$
i.e. $T_{\delta_n}\to\delta$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ (convergence of distributions being, by definition, convergence of the values on each fixed test function). Hence $\bigl(\delta_n\bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}}$ with $\delta_n(x)=\frac n\pi\frac1{1+n^2x^2}$ is a delta sequence, and by $(1.1)$ each member encloses unit area. $\blacksquare$

---

### Remark 1 (alternative ending via dominated convergence)
Step 4 may be replaced by the dominated convergence theorem applied to $(3.1)$: for each fixed $t$ we have $t/n\to0$, so $\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)\to0$ by continuity of $\phi$ at $0$; and $|\phi(t/n)-\phi(0)|/(1+t^{2})\le 2M/(1+t^{2})$, an $n$-independent integrable majorant by $(1.2)$. Hence $E_n\to0$. The $\varepsilon$–$N$ argument was given above to keep the proof elementary and self-contained.

### Remark 2 (what was really used)
Only boundedness of $\phi$ and continuity of $\phi$ at $0$ were used. Consequently $\int_{-\infty}^\infty\delta_n\phi\to\phi(0)$ holds for every bounded $\phi$ that is continuous at $0$ (e.g. every bounded continuous function), test functions being a special case. Note, however, that some hypothesis beyond mere integrability is needed: continuity at $0$ cannot be dropped, since altering $\phi$ at the single point $0$ changes $\phi(0)$ but not any of the integrals.

### Remark 3 (on the figure)
$\delta_n$ is the Lorentzian (Cauchy) profile with peak $\delta_n(0)=n/\pi\to\infty$ and half-width at half-maximum $1/n\to0$ (indeed $\delta_n(x)=\tfrac12\delta_n(0)$ exactly when $|x|=1/n$), while $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\delta_n=1$ for every $n$ by $(1.1)$: the graphs become thinner and taller with unit area, exactly as the picture indicates. Note also that $\delta_n(x)=n\,\delta_1(nx)$, so the family is the standard dilation family generated by the single bump $\delta_1$.
